claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution state.
The initial state has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements without significant Mg segregation.
Thermal treatment causes limited Mg segregation.
Limited Mg segregation promotes nucleation of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-induced localized lattice instabilities drive selective intermetallic nucleation.
Selective nucleation occurs within a narrow temperature window.
Fine Mg-rich precipitates stabilize a protective oxide scale.
Stabilization of the protective oxide scale by fine precipitates improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Prolonged or excessive thermal exposure accelerates precipitate coarsening.
Precipitates may coarsen beyond a critical size or form interconnected networks during continued thermal exposure.
Coarsened or interconnected precipitates compromise passivation and degrade the protective oxide scale.
Fine, dispersed Mg-rich precipitates yield better high-temperature oxidation resistance than the initial homogeneous metastable state.
Fine, dispersed Mg-rich precipitates yield lower corrosion rates than the initial homogeneous metastable state.
Rapid precipitate coarsening causes loss of high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Rapid precipitate coarsening increases corrosion susceptibility.
The protective-to-degraded transition is bounded by a specific temperature interval and limited exposure time.
